name: Clash of Langs
tagline: Pick two of 24 programming languages, give them the same real workload, and compare them with honest statistics.

overview.text: An arena that runs the same computational challenge in two programming languages and compares them. 24 languages are supported, each running as a real native process: CPython, HotSpot, V8, BEAM, GHC-compiled binaries and others. Nothing runs in WebAssembly or as a simulation.

There are 11 challenges, implemented in every language. Data: JSON transform, regex log parsing, group-by aggregation, a CSV sales report and latency analytics. AI and graphics: int8 neural-network inference, RAG-style top-k vector search and an image pipeline. Core: sorting, hash vs binary search and a prime sieve.
Both fighters regenerate the same input from a shared seed and must produce the same checksum; if they do not, the battle is invalid and nobody wins.
Every result is scoped to one workload, one implementation, one runtime and one machine, with the exact versions and command lines attached.
Battles can be replayed exactly from their URL, for example /battle/javascript-vs-go/csv?seed=….

responsibilities.text: Personal open-source project, designed, built and maintained by Alex, covering the Next.js app, the battle engine, the benchmark worker and its Docker image, and the harnesses in all 24 languages.

overview.text: The browser posts a battle configuration to a Next.js route handler and receives a server-sent event stream of battle events.

In production the route handler proxies to a separate benchmark worker, a Docker image with all 24 runtimes on a dedicated host, authenticated with a shared secret header compared in constant time. In local development the engine runs in-process.

The engine takes an exclusive lock, randomises which fighter goes first, and runs each harness under /usr/bin/time to capture peak memory and CPU time. Harnesses stream JSON-line events with in-process monotonic timings for only the timed step.
Every language harness follows a shared contract (bench/SPEC.md), and `npm run bench:verify` checks that all 24 produce byte-identical inputs and outputs for every challenge.
With no worker configured the API returns 503 and the UI shows ARENA OFFLINE; it never substitutes canned numbers.

diagrams.title: How a battle runs
diagrams.source:
flowchart LR
  UI[Browser: Next.js UI + canvas visualisers] -- POST /api/battle, server-sent events --> API[Next.js route handler]
  API -- local dev --> Engine[Battle engine]
  API -- production, BENCH_WORKER_URL --> Worker[Benchmark worker: Docker, all 24 runtimes]
  Worker --> Engine
  Engine -- fixed argv, scrubbed env, timeout, own process group --> H1[bench/lang-A harness]
  Engine --> H2[bench/lang-B harness]
  H1 -- JSON lines: hello, ready, run, done --> Engine
  H2 --> Engine

challenges.title: Making two languages do provably the same work
challenges.problem: Typical language benchmarks do less work in one language, time compilation in another, or report one lucky run.
approach: Each harness regenerates its input from a shared xorshift32 seed and reports an input hash; mismatched hashes invalidate the battle.
Outputs must produce the same checksum, verified across all 24 runtimes by a dedicated script.
Input generation and copies happen outside the timer, so only the challenge itself is measured.

challenges.title: Bit-exact verification for AI and graphics workloads
challenges.problem: Floating-point code legitimately produces slightly different bits across compilers and maths libraries, which would break exact verification.
approach: The AI and graphics challenges use integer arithmetic throughout, as quantised edge inference and classic image pipelines often do.

challenges.title: Running 24 native runtimes from a serverless frontend
challenges.problem: Vercel functions cannot run a JVM, CPython with the harness, or arbitrary native binaries, and shared serverless hardware gives unstable timings.
approach: Vercel hosts only the UI and a thin API.
Execution happens on a dedicated-CPU worker running one container image with every runtime, with cpuset pinned to otherwise idle cores.

challenges.title: Executing processes safely on a public site
challenges.problem: A public page that starts native processes must not let visitors run code, exhaust the host or bypass the API.
approach: Requests carry only a challenge id, two language ids and five integers, which are whitelisted, clamped and passed as argv entries; nothing goes through a shell.
Each process has a 180-second hard timeout, is killed by process group, has a 4 MB stdout cap and runs with a scrubbed environment.
The container runs as non-root with a read-only root filesystem, all capabilities dropped, no-new-privileges, and PID and memory limits.
Per-visitor rate limiting allows 5 battles a minute and 30 an hour, with one battle at a time per worker and a queue depth of 3.

decisions.title: One container with every runtime, on a dedicated VM
decisions.decision: All 24 runtimes ship in one pinned Docker image, run on a dedicated-CPU host.
decisions.rationale: Both fighters get the same hardware and kernel, with pinned versions, which keeps the comparison fair and simple.
alternatives: Browser / WebAssembly: rejected, as it measures each language's WASM build rather than its real runtime.
WASI runtimes: rejected for the same reason, and there is no JVM.
Serverless functions per language: rejected as cold-start dominated, with noisy neighbours and differing hardware.
Firecracker / gVisor per battle: the best isolation, needed only if user-submitted code is ever accepted.
tradeoffs: Needs a dedicated host rather than free serverless hosting; the image is about 2.2 GB.

decisions.title: Medians and significance testing instead of best runs
decisions.decision: The headline is the median of all samples. A winner is declared only if a two-sided Mann–Whitney U test gives p < 0.05; otherwise the battle is a draw.
decisions.rationale: Timings have long right tails, so a non-parametric test is appropriate, and reporting a single fastest run is misleading.
tradeoffs: With fewer than 5 samples per side, significance is unreachable by design.

decisions.title: Flag outliers rather than remove them
decisions.decision: Samples with a modified z-score above 3.5 (Iglewicz & Hoaglin) are flagged in the raw results but still count towards the median.
decisions.rationale: Nothing is cherry-picked; hiding outliers would misrepresent run-to-run variance.

decisions.title: Randomised order and one battle at a time
decisions.decision: The engine holds an exclusive lock per worker, runs fighters sequentially and randomises which goes first.
decisions.rationale: Two benchmarks sharing CPUs measure each other, and a fixed order would systematically give one side the warmer or more throttled slot.

decisions.title: Cold and warm modes
decisions.decision: COLD mode measures fresh-process startup including JIT warm-up; WARM mode measures steady-state throughput after discarded warm-up runs.
decisions.rationale: JIT and adaptive runtimes behave very differently before and after warm-up, so one number cannot describe both.

limitations.text: The worker has no egress firewall yet, and there is no gVisor or Firecracker sandboxing. The project only runs harnesses that ship in the repository and never runs user-submitted code.
Results describe one machine. Runtime versions inside the container differ from a developer Mac, and every result records the exact version it ran on.
CI runs type checking and a production build. Harness correctness is checked by the cross-runtime verification script rather than by a unit-test suite.
Shareable result permalinks and Open Graph result cards are on the roadmap, not yet built.
